title: Voice AI Testing Framework: Regression, Adversarial, and Production-Derived Tests
summary: A voice AI testing framework in three layers: regression, adversarial, and production-derived tests, with what goes in each, its pass rule, and when it runs.
body_markdown:
Without a framework, you end up fixing the same failure twice. Your agent ignores a caller who keeps asking for a person, you patch the prompt, and the next model swap quietly brings the failure back.


A voice AI testing framework is the plan behind your test suite. It decides which simulated calls your agent has to pass, where those calls come from, how often they run, and what result stops a release. We recommend building yours in three layers. Regression tests check that what already works still works. Adversarial tests go looking for the caller, or the audio, that breaks the agent. Production-derived tests turn confirmed failures from real calls into permanent tests.


With all three in place, that ignored request becomes a test, and once the fix passes it moves into the regression suite and runs on every release. Each layer also needs its own pass rule for what counts as passing, because the three kinds of failure need different handling and one pass rate would blur them together. Here’s how the layers differ, and how to build each one.


## Each layer of a voice AI testing framework has its own pass rule


We first laid out this three-layer testing framework in our[2026 Voice AI Report](https://www.coval.ai/2026-voice-ai-report/) . Side by side, the layers look like this.


Layer Question it answers Where cases come from Pass rule When it runs


Regression Does what worked still work? Your top call reasons, must-always behaviors, and fixed failures that graduated Every run of every case passes Every prompt, model, or config change, plus nightly


Adversarial What breaks it? Attack types you can name, and hard audio conditions such as noise and accents One successful attack fails that attack type; hard audio is judged against a clean-call baseline After every agent change, plus a schedule


Production-derived What did real callers find? Confirmed failures from real calls The reproduction fails before the fix and passes after As confirmed failures come in


Together the layers cover the scenarios you know, the edge cases you can anticipate, and the failures nobody anticipated.


Pool the layers into one suite with one pass rate and all three kinds of failure hide. A single leaked account number is a failed release, yet it barely moves an average across hundreds of cases. A drop that shows up only on noisy calls vanishes when noisy and clean calls are scored together. And a reproduced production failure is supposed to fail until its fix ships, so inside the regression gate it keeps the build red for a reason everyone already knows. Separate layers keep each failure where its rule can see it.


## Regression tests keep working behavior working


Regression is the layer that catches a model swap undoing an earlier fix. It holds the calls your agent has to handle correctly every time, and after every change it asks one question: does what worked yesterday still work?


Start with your agent’s top call reasons, then add the behaviors that cut across them, such as authentication, transactions, information lookups, escalation to a human, and recovery from errors. In Coval, these go into a[Regression Set](https://docs.coval.ai/concepts/test-sets/overview) , the scenarios that make up your typical successful calls.


Each test case pairs a goal for the simulated caller with the[expected behaviors](https://docs.coval.ai/concepts/test-sets/evaluation) your agent has to show. The caller never sees those behaviors. After each call, a Coval metric scores every one of them as met or not met. Here’s a case for a clinic’s scheduling agent:


> - **Goal:** move Thursday’s appointment to next week.
> - **Expected behaviors:** verifies the caller’s identity before changing anything; offers open slots; reads back the new date and time; keeps the old booking until the new one is confirmed.


The pass rule is strict. A case passes only when every expected behavior is met on every run. One run isn’t enough, because agents behave differently from one try to the next. Even text agents, with no audio in the way, are inconsistent. In[τ-bench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.12045) , a text benchmark from the AI agent company Sierra, gpt-4o handled simulated retail and airline customer-service tasks and succeeded on fewer than half of them. Its chance of getting a retail task right on all eight tries was under 25%. Coval’s[GitHub Action](https://github.com/coval-ai/coval-github-action) runs each test case up to 10 times and fails your CI job when any simulation returns the failure value you chose for a metric, such as “NO” on a yes/no check.


Run the suite on every prompt, model, or config change, and again every night. At Zoom, a Coval customer, the QA team runs daily scheduled regression tests. Our[regression testing guide](https://www.coval.ai/blog/voice-ai-regression-testing/) goes deeper on building the suite.


## Adversarial tests look for the caller who breaks the agent


Regression only protects what you already know works. Adversarial testing goes looking for the input that makes your agent fail. It comes in two kinds with different pass rules: hostile callers who try to push the agent off policy, and honest callers whose audio, accent, or way of talking trips it up. Red teaming is the hostile half.


**Hostile callers.** Our[red-team guide](https://docs.coval.ai/guides/adversarial-red-team-testing) sorts attacks into 12 types, including identity-verification bypass under pressure, extracting a third party’s personal information, prompt injection, and gradual escalation over many turns. Write a case for each attack type that applies to your agent. For a banking agent, that might be a caller who says they’re the account holder’s spouse and keeps pushing for the balance without passing verification.


The pass rule follows the attacker’s math, since an attacker needs only one success. A scenario passes only when every expected behavior is met, and a single jailbreak, leak, or policy break fails that attack type, even if the average score looks high. Run each scenario at least three times, because an agent that holds once won’t necessarily hold the next time. Attackers retry too. Researchers at Speechmatics and several universities showed this with[Best-of-N jailbreaking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.03556) . The attacker resends the same harmful spoken request with random changes to speed, pitch, noise, and volume until one version gets past the model’s safeguards. It worked on four audio models for 59% to 87% of requests.


**Hard but honest callers.** Our[audio-quality personas](https://docs.coval.ai/guides/testing-across-audio-qualities) include High Background Noise Speaker, Interruptive Speaker, Low Volume Speaker, and Super Fast Speaker, and the[accent guide](https://docs.coval.ai/guides/testing-across-accents) adds six accent personas. Rerun your regression cases under each persona and under Standard Customer, the clean-call baseline, then compare results persona by persona. If a case passes for Standard Customer but fails for High Background Noise Speaker, that’s a failure, even when the overall score holds.


Clean audio tells you little about the noisy call. In our July 2026[speech-to-text benchmark](https://www.coval.ai/blog/word-error-rate-stt-2026/) of 31 models (a 7-day snapshot), no single model led every condition. AssemblyAI Universal 3.5 Pro had the lowest overall word error rate, 3.3%, but OpenAI GPT-4o Transcribe led on accents, intermittent background noise, phone-line compression, and room echo. Task metrics can hide the damage, too. An accented call can score as a success while the recording shows the agent misheard a name, number, or address.


Honest callers also change their minds mid-call. Add cases like “Cancel my order. Actually, can you just change the shipping?” and the caller who asks for an address change and a billing answer in one breath.


Rerun the adversarial suite after every agent change to confirm fixes hold, and on a schedule between releases.


## Production-derived tests turn real failures into permanent tests


Some failures slip past both layers until a real caller hits them, like that ignored request for a person. Production-derived tests start from those calls.


> 1. **Score every production call.** Get your production calls into Coval as[uploaded conversations](https://docs.coval.ai/concepts/uploaded-conversations/overview) , and[Coval’s observability](https://www.coval.ai/products/observability/) scores each one against the metrics you care about.
> 2. **Route flagged calls to people.** An[alert](https://docs.coval.ai/concepts/alerts/overview) on a metric can send calls that cross its threshold straight to a Human Review queue.
> 3. **Confirm the failure.** An automated flag isn’t always a real failure, so have a person check each flagged call before you write a test for it. One team’s[AI-disclosure](https://www.coval.ai/blog/how-to-create-ai-judge-metrics-you-can-trust/) metric, which checks whether the agent says it’s an AI, agreed with human reviewers on 89% of 314 conversations. Every one of the 35 disagreements was a call where the wrong person picked up or the caller hung up early, and the metric had failed the agent for a step the call never reached. In Coval, reviewers confirm flagged calls in a[Triage project](https://docs.coval.ai/concepts/metrics/human-review/human-review) , tagging each one by failure type, theme, and severity.
> 4. **Reproduce it.** Build a test case from the call with a[Transcript input](https://docs.coval.ai/concepts/test-sets/input-types) , where the simulated caller follows the real caller’s side as closely as possible, or an Audio Upload, which replays the real caller audio. For the ignored request, the test replays that call with one expected behavior: transfers the caller to a person when asked.
> 5. **Prove the fix.** The reproduction should fail on the current build. It counts as fixed when it passes on the new one.
> 6. **Generalize.** Write two or three scenario variants of the same failure, so the fix isn’t tuned to one caller’s exact words.


For what to capture from each call, see[voice AI observability](https://www.coval.ai/blog/what-is-voice-ai-observability/) .


## How cases move between layers, and how many you need


Once a fix is proved, the case moves. An adversarial finding or a confirmed production failure graduates into the regression suite, and from then on it runs on every change, model swaps included.[Krew](https://www.coval.ai/blog/how-krew-runs-10-000-voice-ai-evaluations-monthly-with-coval-(and-turns-qa-into-sales-acceleration)/) , a Coval customer, works this way: “Whenever there’s an edge case, we add it into our eval set and run it again.”


*How a confirmed failure becomes a permanent regression test, so you fix it once.*


Cases also go stale. Self-driving evaluation, where our approach to testing started, has a name for it:[scenario decay](https://www.coval.ai/blog/improve-agent-performance-with-voice-benchmarks-ama-replay/) . A scenario written to measure one thing stops measuring it. In voice AI, it’s a test of identity capture where the phone number no longer works, so the call never reaches the identity step. A decayed case fails for reasons that have nothing to do with the agent, or passes without testing anything, so fix it or delete it.


Size each layer from your own agent, not from a target count:


> - **Regression:** one case per must-always behavior across your top call reasons, plus every fix that graduated.
> - **Adversarial:** a case for each attack type that applies to your agent, plus your regression cases rerun under each audio and accent condition your callers bring.
> - **Production-derived:** one case per confirmed failure, plus its variants. This layer grows with your traffic.


Two things sit outside the three layers. How your agent holds up under many simultaneous calls gets its own[load testing](https://www.coval.ai/blog/voice-load-testing/) plan, and choosing what to score is covered in our[evaluation guide](https://www.coval.ai/blog/voice-ai-agent-evaluation-guide/) .


## Coval runs all three layers in one loop


Moving cases between layers only works if a failure is measured the same way everywhere it shows up. In Coval,[every metric](https://docs.coval.ai/concepts/metrics/overview) works on both simulated conversations and live-monitored production calls. The metric that flagged a live failure is the one that scores its reproduction and, later, its regression case, so a pass means the same thing at every stage.


[Scheduled runs](https://docs.coval.ai/concepts/runs/overview) keep the layers going without anyone kicking them off: the regression suite every night, the adversarial suite between releases. A schedule can be anything from every 15 minutes to every 30 days. And the Coval CLI takes you from install to your first simulation in[under 15 minutes](https://docs.coval.ai/welcome) .


That’s the whole framework. Three layers, each with its own pass rule, and a loop that turns every fixed failure into a regression test. It’s what lets you fix that ignored request for a person once and know it stays fixed.
